fixes.explanation: The LORD tells Isaiah, “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz.” Those are the same words He told Isaiah to write on the scroll back in verse 1. So the name on the scroll is the name for the boy.
Ahaz is the king of Judah the LORD sends Isaiah to speak to (Isaiah 7:3-4). But for this baby, the instruction is “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz.” That's the name from the scroll in verse 1.
I get the hopeful thought, but the LORD says the opposite. Nothing gets handed back in this verse. The wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria.

Nice try, but hiding isn't in this verse. The LORD says the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off, and the king of Assyria is the one doing the carrying. "Hidden away" just isn't what the text says.

It's actually true. The LORD says this people rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and the son of Remaliah. Rezin was king of Aram, and the son of Remaliah was Pekah, king of Israel (Isaiah 7:1). I think it's an easy one to doubt, since cheering for those two kings is a surprising move.

No famine is mentioned in these verses. The Lord says He will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates. The whole picture is a river overflowing its channels and overrunning its banks. Famine isn't part of the picture in verse 7.

That's the one. The flood "…will pour into Judah, swirling and sweeping over it, reaching up to the neck…" Judah is the land where Ahaz is king (Isaiah 7:1). The streams spread until they cover the entire land.
Moab isn't in this passage at all. The flood pours into Judah, and its spreading streams cover the entire land. Judah is the land where Ahaz is king (Isaiah 7:1). So the water's address is Judah.
Yes. The message says, "prepare for battle, and be shattered; prepare for battle, and be shattered!" Huddling together and preparing for battle both end in the same word. The answer is shattered.

That's a nice thought, but the message says the opposite. The peoples are told to huddle together and prepare for battle, and the text says they will be shattered. It says it more than once, so there's no room for a win. If anything, this is the loudest 'no' in the passage.
